name: ns-3
why: A real discrete-event network simulator used in research, letting you model protocols and traffic at home.

brief.what_it_is: ns-3 is a discrete-event network simulator for Internet systems, per its homepage. It is free, open-source software under the GNU GPLv2, maintained by a worldwide community. The pages describe it as aimed mainly at research and education. The current release is ns-3.49, distributed as a source archive of the mainline code, with a companion ns-allinone bundle that adds contributed modules. The fetched pages do not describe the inputs or outputs of a typical run.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames ns-3 as a simulator for Internet systems, targeted primarily for research and educational use. It does not state a broader motivation in the pages I read.
brief.install_notes: The fetched pages gave no install commands or first-run steps. The ns-3.49 download is a source archive of the mainline code. An ns-allinone release bundles compatible contributed modules with the mainline release. Documentation for contributed modules is not hosted on nsnam.org. The release page links to release notes, changes, errata, an upgrade patch from 3.48 to 3.49, and documentation in several formats.
brief.standout: The release notes show a large, actively developed model library. ns-3.49 adds 3GPP TR 38.901 inter-UE spatial consistency and large-bandwidth/large-antenna-array modeling, an 8-11x speedup of the 3GPP channel model, a Flent application, Wi-Fi IBSS beaconing, and 6LoWPAN and Zigbee additions. The 3GPP channel and Wi-Fi models stand out among its many protocol models.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage lists ns-3.49 released Oct 7, 2026, ns-3.48 released Jun 2, 2026, and ns-allinone-3.48 released Aug 10, 2026. The homepage also mentions the 2026 International Conference on ns-3 (Oct 19-21, Naples) and participation in Google Summer of Code 2026. A follow-on ns-allinone-3.49 is planned for later in October.
brief.caveats: I found no install instructions in the pages I read, so build and setup steps are unknown from these notes. Contributed-module docs live outside nsnam.org. The homepage does not mention home use or consumer-level simulation, so the scout note about modeling protocols and traffic at home is not confirmed by these pages.

entry.title: ns-3
entry.tldr: A discrete-event network simulator used in research and teaching, where you model Wi-Fi, cellular and Internet protocols in software instead of on real hardware.
entry.deeper_look:
ns-3 is a discrete-event network simulator for Internet systems. Its homepage says it is "targeted primarily for research and educational use." It is free, open-source software under GPLv2, maintained by a worldwide community.

The idea underneath is the discrete-event simulation. Instead of running real packets over real wires, the simulator keeps a queue of timestamped events, such as a packet being sent, a frame arriving, or a timer firing. It jumps from one event to the next. That lets you model networks you could never build at home and run them far faster or slower than real time, with repeatable results.

The model library is large and still growing. According to the release notes, ns-3.49 adds 3GPP TR 38.901 inter-UE spatial consistency, large-bandwidth and large-antenna-array modeling, and an 8-11x speedup of the 3GPP channel model. It also adds a Flent application, Wi-Fi IBSS beaconing, and 6LoWPAN and Zigbee additions. The Wi-Fi and 3GPP channel models are the standouts in a long list of protocol models.

The release is distributed as a source archive of the mainline code. A companion ns-allinone bundle adds compatible contributed modules. The pages the brief draws on do not describe what a typical run takes in or produces, so expect to start from the project's documentation and tutorials.
entry.install:
brew install ns-3
# The formula depends on open-mpi. Upstream also distributes source archives (mainline, and an ns-allinone bundle with contributed modules) from nsnam.org.
entry.whats_unique: It is a real research-grade simulator with a broad, actively developed library of protocol models, from Wi-Fi to 3GPP cellular to Zigbee, that you can run on your own machine.
entry.caveats: The brew formula installs no executables, and the pages I read gave no first-run steps, so expect to work from the upstream documentation; contributed-module docs are hosted outside nsnam.org.
